title: Constitutionalism and the Rule of Law

blocks.text: Almost every military regime in history has published a constitution. Having a rulebook has never stopped a government from doing as it pleases. What matters is whether the rulers can actually be **stopped** — whether a court can tell a president he has broken the law and be obeyed. That difference is the difference between having a constitution and practising constitutionalism.

blocks.title: Constitutionalism
blocks.text: The doctrine that government power must be exercised within known legal limits, and that those limits are effectively enforced. A state practises constitutionalism when rulers actually submit to the constitution, when their powers are checked by other institutions, and when citizens can obtain a remedy against the government in an independent court.

blocks.markdown: The distinction examiners look for is this: a **constitution** is a document or set of rules, while **constitutionalism** is a practice. A country can have an elaborate written constitution and no constitutionalism at all — this was Nigeria's position under military rule, when decrees suspended parts of the constitution and ousted the courts' jurisdiction. Equally, Britain has no codified constitution yet a long tradition of constitutionalism.

items: **A supreme constitution** that binds the rulers as well as the ruled.
**Limited government** — powers are defined, and what is not granted is withheld.
**Separation of powers** with real checks and balances between the three organs.
**An independent judiciary** able to declare an act of government unlawful.
**Regular, free and fair elections** so that rulers can be changed peacefully.
**Accountability and transparency** in the use of public power and public money.
**A free press and an active civil society** to expose abuse.

blocks.markdown:
### The rule of law

The **rule of law** means that a state is governed by settled law rather than by the arbitrary will of those in power. Its classic formulation comes from the English jurist **A. V. Dicey**, who set out three principles:

1. **Absence of arbitrary power.** No one may be punished except for a definite breach of law established in the ordinary courts. Government must be able to point to a legal authority for whatever it does.
2. **Equality before the law.** Every person, whatever their rank or office, is subject to the same law administered by the same courts. There is no separate law for officials.
3. **Rights grounded in ordinary law.** The liberties of the citizen are secured by the decisions of the courts in actual cases rather than by mere declarations on paper.

items: **Impartiality and independence of the judiciary**, so that the law is applied without fear or favour.
**Fair hearing** — the right to be heard, to know the charge, to a lawyer, and to be tried by an unbiased court, guaranteed by section 36 of the 1999 Constitution.
**Presumption of innocence** until guilt is proved.
**No retroactive criminal legislation** — an act cannot be made a crime after it has been done.
**Right of appeal** to a higher court.
**Legal certainty** — laws must be published, clear and prospective.
**Right to seek redress** against the state, provided by section 46, which gives any person who alleges a breach of Chapter IV rights direct access to a High Court.

blocks.markdown:
### Fundamental human rights in the 1999 Constitution

**Chapter IV**, sections 33 to 46, contains the justiciable fundamental rights. These are the rights a Nigerian can actually enforce in court.

rows: Right to dignity of the human person, prohibiting torture, inhuman treatment and slavery
Right to private and family life, including home and correspondence
Right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Right to freedom of expression and the press
Right to peaceful assembly and association
Right to acquire and own immovable property anywhere in Nigeria
blocks.caption: Chapter IV rights, 1999 Constitution. Section 44 protects against compulsory acquisition of property without compensation, section 45 permits lawful restrictions, and section 46 provides the remedy

blocks.title: Chapter II rights are not enforceable
blocks.text: Chapter II of the 1999 Constitution, sections 13 to 24, sets out the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy — goals such as free education, adequate shelter and suitable employment. These are **not** justiciable: section 6(6)(c) expressly removes them from the jurisdiction of the courts. They are duties of conscience on the government, not rights a citizen can sue on. Only Chapter IV rights can be enforced in court.

blocks.markdown:
### Limitations on rights and obstacles to the rule of law

No right is absolute. **Section 45** allows laws that are reasonably justifiable in a democratic society to restrict certain rights in the interest of defence, public safety, public order, public morality or public health, or to protect the rights of other persons. **Section 305** permits a President to proclaim a state of emergency, during which some rights may be derogated from.

Beyond these lawful limits, the rule of law faces practical obstacles:

- **Delegated legislation and wide discretionary powers** granted to officials.
- **Immunity clauses** — section 308 shields the President, Vice-President, Governors and Deputy Governors from civil and criminal proceedings while in office.
- **Diplomatic immunity** enjoyed by accredited foreign envoys.
- **Military rule and decrees**, which historically suspended constitutional provisions and ousted judicial review.
- **Poverty, illiteracy and the high cost of litigation**, which put the courts out of reach of ordinary citizens.
- **Delay in the courts** and executive disobedience of court orders.
- **Corruption** in the police, prosecution and judiciary.

blocks.title: Evaluating a government action against the rule of law
blocks.prompt: A state governor orders the police to demolish a market at dawn without notice, and to detain the traders' union leader for three weeks without charge to stop protests. Evaluate this action against the principles of the rule of law and the 1999 Constitution.

steps.text: Identify the rights engaged. Demolition without notice touches section 43, the right to acquire and own immovable property, and section 44, which forbids compulsory acquisition of property without prompt payment of compensation. Detention for three weeks without charge engages section 35, the right to personal liberty.

Apply Dicey's first principle, the absence of arbitrary power. Section 35(4) and (5) require a detained person to be brought before a court within a reasonable time, generally 24 or 48 hours depending on the distance to the nearest court. Three weeks with no charge is therefore arbitrary detention.

Apply the fair hearing requirement in section 36. Demolishing the market at dawn without notice denies the traders any chance to be heard before losing their property, breaching the principle that no one should be condemned unheard.

Consider whether section 45 saves the action. It permits restrictions reasonably justifiable in a democratic society in the interest of public order. Silencing a protest leader is not a legitimate public-order purpose, and no lawful procedure was followed, so section 45 does not apply.

State the remedy. Under section 46 the traders and the union leader may apply directly to the High Court of the state, or the Federal High Court, for enforcement of their fundamental rights, seeking release, a declaration and compensation.

Conclude with the constitutionalism point. The existence of these constitutional provisions is not enough on its own; the rule of law is only vindicated if the court's order is actually obeyed by the governor.

blocks.answer: The action breaches sections 35, 36, 43 and 44, and violates Dicey's principles of absence of arbitrary power and equality before the law. Section 45 offers no defence, and redress lies under section 46 — but only genuine compliance with the court's order would demonstrate constitutionalism

blocks.title: Two marks that are easily lost
blocks.text: First, never say a country "has no rule of law because it has no constitution" — Britain disproves it. Second, do not list free education or adequate shelter among the fundamental rights a Nigerian can enforce. Those sit in Chapter II and are expressly non-justiciable under section 6(6)(c).

points: A constitution is a set of rules; constitutionalism is the practice of rulers actually submitting to those rules and being effectively checked.
Constitutionalism requires a supreme constitution, limited government, separation of powers, an independent judiciary, enforceable rights, free elections and accountability.
The rule of law means government by settled law rather than arbitrary will.
Dicey's three principles are absence of arbitrary power, equality before the law, and rights grounded in decisions of the ordinary courts.
Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution, sections 33 to 46, contains the fundamental rights that can be enforced in court.
Chapter II, sections 13 to 24, contains Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles which section 6(6)(c) makes non-justiciable.
Section 45 permits lawful restrictions on rights, and section 305 allows derogation during a state of emergency.
The rule of law is obstructed in practice by wide discretionary powers, the section 308 immunity clause, military decrees, poverty, court delay and corruption.
